In this work, we offer a comprehensive definition of the role of ChaaS provider, and we find ChaaS to be a flexible means for directing public and/or private investments toward the efficient rollout of charging infrastructure. No comprehensive and non-commercial survey of ChaaS business cases as they appear in the market is currently available to the public. Many potential but yet-unrealized benefits of ChaaS are asserted by commercial providers, but no examples analyzing these asserted benefits are found in the current literature. This chapter provides an overview of what we understand to be the purpose and functions of ChaaS, economic analyses of four potential use cases for ChaaS, and discussion of the various types of benefits ChaaS can provide to the transportation and energy systems to enable increased adoption of EVs. System model of Charging-as-a-Service ChaaS exists at the interface between providers of electric power and EV operators, or, put broadly, the interface between the electricity and transportation systems. The electrification of transportation involves establishing a new type and scope of interface between these systems in the form of vehicle charging. Under dominant EV charging models, this interface is a locus of confusion, miscommunication, and general inefficiency, because it is where the motivations and imperatives of the two previously disconnected systems must be coordinated. For example, EV drivers benefit from speed and flexibility in charging, whereas electric power providers benefit from predictability and stability in power demand. These incentives can contradict one another, and their reconciliation is likely to tip in favor of one side or the other depending on regulations, power dynamics, and other factors. If electricity providers assess electricity prices on an energy basis ($/kilowatt-hour, kWh) irrespective of time or power demand, which is typical of residential price structures, charging flexibility is incentivized at the risk of distribution system stability (for example, if many EVs charge simultaneously in the same neighborhood and overload the local distribution infrastructure26). On the other hand, if electricity prices include an expensive peak demand price, which is typical of commercial price structures, users may be incentivized to forgo high-power or simultaneous charging, which may handicap the transportation function of their EVs by necessitating long dwell times.
